prose romance by Daṇḍin. The main part of the current Daśakumāracarita perhaps formed part of this voluminous Avantisundarī.
MT. 3454 (a. (full of lacunae). TCD. VIII. 1349. Tra. Ad. Rep. [Page419-a. 1100. 3 (inc.). Trav. Uni. 1086B. T. 704 (both inc.). The Madras fr. has appeared in print in the Dakṣiṇa Bhāratī Series, Madras. This Avantisundarīya of Daṇḍin is q. in the Nāmasaṁgrahamālā of Appayya Dīkṣita. See Annals of Ori. Res., Uni. of Mad, Vol. V. No. 2. The Trivandram Curator's Office has a transcript of a portion of this work, forming the beginning, without however the introductory verses. The following information is based on a. examination of the Triv. Cur.'s transcript:
The ms. begins abruptly towards the end of the description of Kañcī, p. 6. Mentions the Pallava king Siṁhaviṣṇu to whom a Gandharva addresses a. Āryā. Asked about the a. of the Āryā, the Gandharva narrates: From Ānandapura in Āryadeśa a Brahman family migrated to Acalapura created by Mūladeva (the founder of Kitavasiddhānta) for his friend Acala, in the vicinity of Nāsik; it was a Kauśika gotra family; in it appeared Narāyaṇasvāmin an. his son was Damodarasvāmin (ref. to a. Kauśikakumāra). Dāmodara became a great friend of the Mahāśaiva, of great power an. the source of poesy, Bharavi, an. following the latter, established friendship with prince (Rājasūnu) Viṣṇuvardhana (Kubja Viṣṇuvardhana) an. accompanied the latter during a hunt; in the hunt, Dāmodara had to take meat an. consequently had to perform a Tīrthayātra; during his Yātrā, Dāmodara came into contact with the Gāṅga king Durvinīta who was known for his wanderings (bhramaṇaśīlakīrteh2). Dāmodara was twenty years of age a. [Page419-b] that time; he was the a. of the Āryā which the Gandharva addressed to Pallava Siṁhaviṣṇu a. Kāñcī. Pallava Siṁhaviṣṇu then invited Dāmodara to his own court through repeated Śrīmukhas (anekaśrīmukhākṛṣṭamenam ātmasād akarot) an., so to say, adopted him a. his own son an. gave him a Brahmadeya village.
Dāmodara's literary achievements a. this juncture are thus ref. to: (caturAnanasya AdikaveH dvijottamasya prAkRtAnAM ca vastubhedAnAM tatpUrva prakaTayituH tasya (dAmodarasya)). Once Dāmodara sent some Pkt. songs (prākṛtagānāni) to Siṁhaviṣṇu. Dāmodara then wrote the work Gandhamādana an. a Lakṣaṇa-grantha for Skt. an. Pkt. poetry.
sa ca tathAnugRhyamANo gandhamAdanaprabhRtibhiH varakRtaiH saMskRtaprAkRtAnAM ca kAvyAnAM lakSaNaiH dakSiNApathaM sanAthamakarot | At the instance of the king, Dāmodara married; three sons were born to him: Siṁhaviṣṇu, Manoratha, Atilobha.
Manoratha the second son had four sons: Dāmodara, Bhavadāsa, Siṁhaviṣṇu, Vīradatta.
Vīradatta the last, married Gaurī of Māṭhara gotra an. begot many daughters an. a. long last, a son named DAṆḌIN. When Daṇḍin was still a child, the mother passed away an. soon after Daṇḍin's Upanayana, his father also passed away.
An invasion of the Tamil (Pallavacountry now took place an. the Dramilas (Pallavas), Colas an. Pāṇḍyas were all affected: there was devastation, pillage an. famine. Daṇḍin left his home an. wandered over several places, staying in a number of Gurukulas. Invited by the Pallava king to [Page420-a. come back, Daṇḍin returned to his native place.
Daṇḍin was once invited by a Sthapati, architect, named Lalitālaya, pupil of Māndhātā, who was a. expert in building yantras. Lalitālaya was himself a. expert in manufacturing military machines an. besides, was a. author in Tamil, having written in that language the Śūdrakacarita. (amunA kila dramiDabhASayA zUdakacaritamupanibaddham). Lalitālaya invited Daṇḍin to Mahāmallapuram to see how he had effected a joint in the broken arm of the Śeṣaśayana image there.
At that time Daṇḍin's friend an. son of the general Raṇamalla, Vīrapatāka, spoke. Mention is then made of a Bhavanātha described a. a Kalpasūtra-ṭīkākāra an. his son a great Māheśvara an. ‘Mantrārtha-tattvavyākhyāna-catura’, named Mātṛdatta. There is a gap in the text here; evidently Mātṛdatta follows Daṇḍin to Mahāmallapuram.
At Mahāmallapuram they see the palace on the sea-shore, an. see an. admire Lalitālaya's workmanship on the arm of the image. At this juncture, a huge red lotus floats up from the sea, touches the feet of the image, changes into a divine form an. vanishes heavenwards.
On seeing this, another friend of Daṇḍin, Rāmaśarman, a native of Coladeśa speaks. Daṇḍin thinks that a sage must have cursed a divine being to become a lotus like that. The party Daṇḍin, Mātṛdatta, Rāmaśarma an. Vimata (Vīrapatāka ?) then return to Kāñcī. [Page420-b]
Daṇḍin then has a dream in which Sarasvatī blesses him an. asks him to write the story of the Vidyādhara king Rājavāhana. Next morning, Daṇḍin narrates the story of Avantisundarī, which he saw in his dream-vision.
The following works are mentioned during the story in the Trivandrum fr.
--Bṛhatkathā, Setubandha, Kādambarī, Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata; Auśanasa, Bārhaspatya, Vaiśālākṣa an. Bāhudantaka Artha Śāstras.
The above Intro. to the story gives the contemporaneity of Bhāravi, (Eastern Cālukya) Kubja Viṣṇuvardhana, (Gāṅga) Durvinīta, (Pallava) Siṁhaviṣṇu, an. Poet Dāmodara, the last being the great-grandfather of Daṇḍin.
